description: Fill January before December goes quiet. A six-week plan from mid-November to the new year, 9 ready-to-send emails for year-end budget, Q1 planning, past clients and holiday hours, a prepaid work block offer with paste-in terms, a full worked example, an outreach tracker and a Q1 booking calendar.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Year-End Booking Kit

December is when a lot of freelance calendars quietly empty out. Clients go on holiday, decisions slide "to the new year", and January starts with an empty pipeline and a gap in income that shows up in February. This kit helps you use the last six weeks of the year to do two things: pick up any year-end work that clients still want done, and fill your January and February before the holidays start.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `six-week-plan.md` | A week-by-week plan from mid-November to the first week of January | Read first; follow it from whatever week you're in |
| `client-emails.md` | 9 ready-to-send emails: year-end budget, Q1 planning, past clients, holiday hours, follow-ups | Weeks 1-5 |
| `prepaid-block-offer.md` | How to offer a pre-paid block of work a client can buy now and use in Q1, with terms you can paste | When a client mentions budget to spend |
| `worked-example.md` | One designer's six weeks, start to finish, with the numbers | Read once before you start |
| `outreach-tracker.csv` | One row per client or contact you reach out to | Every day you send an email |
| `q1-booking-calendar.csv` | Your January-February weeks, with capacity, what's booked and what's tentative | Update after every yes or maybe |

## How to use it in 30 minutes

1. **Make your list (10 min).** Open `outreach-tracker.csv`. Add every current client, every client you worked with in the last two years, and every warm lead that went quiet. Most people find 15-40 names.
2. **Block your calendar (10 min).** Open `q1-booking-calendar.csv` and fill in the "capacity_days" column for each week of January and February. Be honest about holidays and admin time.
3. **Send the first three emails (10 min).** Pick the three warmest names and send the matching email from `client-emails.md`. Log them in the tracker.

Then follow `six-week-plan.md`: about 20-30 minutes a day of outreach and follow-up.

## The three ideas behind this kit

- **Ask before the shutdown, not after.** Once people leave for the holidays, nothing gets approved until mid-January. A "let's plan Q1" conversation in late November is easy; the same conversation on January 12th competes with everyone else's.
- **Give clients a reason to decide now.** "Let me know if you need anything" gets ignored. A specific suggestion ("I could do the spring campaign assets in the first two weeks of January, want me to hold those dates?") gets answers.
- **Write down every maybe.** Tentative holds are where January work comes from. The tracker and calendar make sure none of them go cold.

## A note on prepaid work and taxes

Taking payment in December for work done in January can change which tax year the income lands in, and some clients have their own rules about prepaying. This kit gives general information only. If the amounts matter to you, check with an accountant or tax adviser where you live before you sell a prepaid block.

## Works with

The `.csv` files open in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice. The `.md` files open in any text editor, and look best in an app that shows Markdown (Notion, Obsidian, Typora, or a code editor's preview).

## License

For your own use in your own freelance business. You can edit and send the emails as your own. Please don't resell or share the kit itself.

# Year-End Client Emails

Nine emails, in the order you'll usually send them. Replace everything in [square brackets]. Keep them short: every one of these should be readable on a phone in under 30 seconds.

Tips that apply to all of them:
- Put one specific suggestion in every email. "Anything you need?" is easy to ignore; "Want me to take the spring catalog in January?" is easy to answer.
- Give a date. People decide faster when there's a real reason to.
- One email, one question.

---

## Email 1: Year-end budget (current clients)

**Subject:** Anything to wrap up before year-end?

Hi [Name],

As we head into December, I wanted to check whether you have any work you'd like done, or budget you'd like to use, before the end of the year.

A couple of things I could take on in the next few weeks:
- [Specific suggestion 1, e.g. "refresh the homepage banners for January"]
- [Specific suggestion 2, e.g. "turn the Q3 report into a one-page summary"]

I have [number] days free between now and [date your break starts]. If it's easier, I can also set up a prepaid block of [hours/days] that you buy now and use any time in [Q1 / the first quarter].

Would either of those help?

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 2: Q1 planning (current clients)

**Subject:** Planning [Month] together

Hi [Name],

I'm starting to plan my January and February and wanted to make sure I keep room for you.

Is anything coming up early in the year that I could help with? I was thinking about [specific project, e.g. "the spring product launch you mentioned"], which would need to start around [date] to be ready by [date].

If it's useful, I'm happy to do a 20-minute call before the holidays to map it out. [Two or three time options.]

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 3: Past client check-in

**Subject:** [Their company] + [something specific]

Hi [Name],

It's been a while since we worked on [past project], and I noticed [something real and recent: a new product, a hiring post, a redesign, an announcement]. Congratulations.

I'm booking projects for January and February now. If you have anything like [type of work you did for them] on the list for early next year, I'd be glad to help, and I can hold some dates for you before my calendar fills.

Either way, I hope the year has gone well.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 4: Warm lead revival

**Subject:** Still thinking about [project]?

Hi [Name],

We spoke in [month] about [project]. I know timing wasn't right then.

If it's back on the table for the new year, I have some availability in [January/February] and could put together an updated plan and quote before the holidays, so you can start straight away in January.

Would that be useful? A one-word reply is fine.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 5: Holiday hours

**Subject:** My holiday hours

Hi [Name],

A quick note so nothing gets stuck over the holidays:

- **Last working day:** [date]
- **Back:** [date]
- **For anything urgent before then,** please send it by [date, usually 3-5 working days before your last day] so I can finish it before the break.

[If they have work booked:] Your [project] is scheduled to start on [date], and I'll be in touch on [date] with anything I need from you.

Thanks for a great year.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 6: Gentle follow-up (no reply)

**Subject:** Re: [original subject]

Hi [Name],

Just bringing this back to the top of your inbox in case it got buried. Even a "not this year" is helpful so I can plan.

Best,
[Your name]

Send 5 working days after the first email. If there's still no reply after another 7 working days, mark it "no reply" in the tracker and try again in January with Email 9's follow-up line.

---

## Email 7: Hold the dates

**Subject:** Holding [dates] for [project]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for the chat about [project]. To make sure we can start when you want, I've pencilled in:

- **Start:** [date]
- **First draft / milestone:** [date]
- **Finish:** [date]

I can hold these dates until [confirm-by date, usually 7-10 days out]. After that I'll need to release them for other work. To confirm, just reply "confirmed" and I'll send [the agreement / the deposit invoice] over.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 8: Last call before the break

**Subject:** Before I sign off for the year

Hi [Name],

I'm finishing up for the year on [date]. Before I do, I wanted to check in on [project/conversation].

If you'd like me to keep [dates] for you in January, I just need a quick yes by [date]. If it's a "later in the year" kind of thing, no problem, just let me know and I'll check back in [month].

Best,
[Your name]

---

## Email 9: January kickoff

**Subject:** Kicking off [project] on [date]

Hi [Name],

Happy new year. I'm all set to start [project] on [date] as planned.

Before then, could you send me:
- [Item 1, e.g. "the final product photos"]
- [Item 2, e.g. "access to the shared drive"]
- [Item 3, e.g. "the name of the person who signs off on drafts"]

Our first check-in is [date and time]. I'll send an agenda the day before.

Best,
[Your name]

**Restart line for anyone who didn't reply in December** (add as the first line of a fresh email):
"I know December was busy for everyone. I'm planning the next few weeks now and wanted to check back on [project]."

files.prepaid-block-offer.md:
# The Prepaid Block Offer

Some clients reach December with budget they need to commit before the year ends, but no project ready to start. A prepaid block lets them buy a set amount of your time now and use it early next year. You get cash and booked work in a quiet season; they get a supplier lined up and their budget used.

Not every client can do this. Some organizations don't allow paying for work before it's delivered. Offer it, don't push it.

---

## Step 1: Decide the size

Pick one or two sizes, not five. Simple choices get faster answers.

| Size | Good for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Small block | Clients who send small jobs often | 10 hours |
| Large block | Clients with a known Q1 project | 5 days (or 40 hours) |

Use whatever unit you already bill in: hours, days, or deliverables.

## Step 2: Decide the price

Three common options. Pick one and use it for every client.

1. **Your normal rate.** Simplest. The benefit to the client is guaranteed dates and a used budget.
2. **A small discount (5-10%)** for paying in full upfront. Only if you'd be glad to get the cash now at that price.
3. **Normal rate plus a bonus** (for example, a free 30-minute planning call in January). Keeps your rate intact.

Avoid big discounts. A prepaid block is not a sale; it's a convenience for both sides.

## Step 3: Set the rules

Write these down before you offer it, so every client gets the same deal. Fill in the blanks:

- **Use-by date:** Block must be used by [date, e.g. March 31].
- **What it covers:** [Types of work, e.g. "any design or copy work in my usual services"].
- **How time is tracked:** [e.g. "in 15-minute increments; I'll send a balance with every invoice/update"].
- **Scheduling:** [e.g. "Book work with at least 5 working days' notice. Larger projects are scheduled together."].
- **Unused time:** [Choose one: "Unused time at the use-by date expires" / "Unused time can be extended once by 30 days" / "Unused time is refunded at the rate paid"].
- **Overruns:** [e.g. "Work beyond the block is billed at my normal rate, and I'll tell you before we go over."].

## Step 4: Terms you can paste

Adjust to fit your contract. If you already have a contract with the client, attach this as a short addendum or statement of work.

> **Prepaid Work Block**
>
> [Client] is purchasing a prepaid block of [10 hours / 5 days] of [your services] from [Your name/business] at [rate], for a total of [amount], payable on invoice by [date].
>
> The block can be used for work requested between [start date] and [use-by date]. Work is scheduled by agreement, with at least [5] working days' notice. Time is tracked in [15-minute] increments, and a running balance is included with each update.
>
> Work beyond the block is billed at [normal rate] after written approval. [Unused time policy.]
>
> All other terms of our existing agreement dated [date] apply.

## Step 5: Invoice and track

- Send the invoice as soon as the client confirms. Put "Prepaid work block, [hours/days], valid until [date]" on the line item.
- Add a row to `q1-booking-calendar.csv` as **prepaid** so you remember the time is sold.
- Every time you use part of the block, send the balance: "This took 2.5 hours. Remaining: 7.5 of 10 hours, valid until March 31."

## Taxes and accounting (general information only)

Being paid in one year for work you do in the next can affect when the income counts for tax, and the rules differ by country and by how you do your accounts. Some places also treat prepayments differently for sales tax or VAT. This is not tax advice: if the amount is significant, ask an accountant before you send the invoice.

## When not to offer it

- You don't have room in Q1 to honour it.
- The client has a history of paying late or changing scope a lot.
- You'd spend the cash before doing the work and leave yourself short in Q1.

files.six-week-plan.md:
# Six-Week Year-End Booking Plan

This plan runs from mid-November to the first working week of January. If you're starting late, jump to the week you're in and do that week's "must do" items first. Each week takes about 2-3 hours in total, spread over short daily sessions.

Times below assume a Northern Hemisphere calendar where most clients slow down from around December 18th and come back around January 5th. Shift the weeks to match your clients' holidays.

---

## Week 1 (mid-November): Build the list and set your dates

**Goal:** know who you're contacting and what you're offering.

Must do:
- [ ] Fill in `outreach-tracker.csv` with every current client, past client (last 24 months) and warm lead.
- [ ] Mark each one with a `group`: **current**, **past**, or **lead**.
- [ ] Fill in `q1-booking-calendar.csv`: capacity for each week of January and February. Leave a buffer: if you can do 5 days a week, plan for 4.
- [ ] Decide your holiday dates and write them down. You'll need them for the holiday-hours email.
- [ ] Decide if you'll offer a prepaid block (see `prepaid-block-offer.md`). If yes, set the size and price now.

Nice to have:
- [ ] Write one line per current client about what they might need in Q1 (a launch, a new season, a report, a redesign). This becomes the "specific suggestion" in your emails.

---

## Week 2: Current clients first

**Goal:** catch year-end budget and get a Q1 planning conversation on the calendar.

Must do:
- [ ] Send **Email 1 (year-end budget)** to current clients whose budgets run on a calendar year, or who have mentioned budget before.
- [ ] Send **Email 2 (Q1 planning)** to every other current client.
- [ ] Log each send in the tracker with the date and `next_step_date` 5 working days later.

Why current clients first: they already trust you, they're the fastest to say yes, and their answers tell you how much January capacity you have left for everyone else.

---

## Week 3: Past clients and warm leads

**Goal:** reopen doors before the holiday break.

Must do:
- [ ] Send **Email 3 (past client check-in)** to past clients. Personalize the first line with something real: their last project, a change you've seen on their website, a recent announcement.
- [ ] Send **Email 4 (warm lead revival)** to leads who went quiet.
- [ ] Follow up on Week 2 emails with no reply using **Email 6 (gentle follow-up)**.
- [ ] Move every "yes" or "maybe" into `q1-booking-calendar.csv` as **booked** or **tentative**.

---

## Week 4 (early December): Confirm and hold dates

**Goal:** turn maybes into dates.

Must do:
- [ ] For every tentative project, send **Email 7 (hold the dates)** with specific January dates and a deadline for the client to confirm.
- [ ] Send **Email 5 (holiday hours)** to all current clients and anyone with a booked or tentative project.
- [ ] If anyone bought a prepaid block, send an invoice and a short written summary of what it covers (see `prepaid-block-offer.md`).

---

## Week 5 (mid-December): Last call before the break

**Goal:** close what can be closed; set up January for the rest.

Must do:
- [ ] Send **Email 8 (last call before the break)** to anyone with an open conversation.
- [ ] Release tentative holds that passed their confirm-by date, and tell the client you've done so (it often prompts a yes).
- [ ] Write January's first-week task list so you start on day one, not day three.
- [ ] Update the tracker: every row should have a `status` and a `next_step_date` in January if it's still open.

---

## Week 6 (first working week of January): Kick off

**Goal:** start booked work on time and restart the open conversations.

Must do:
- [ ] Send **Email 9 (January kickoff)** to every booked client, confirming start dates and what you need from them.
- [ ] Follow up every open row in the tracker whose `next_step_date` has arrived.
- [ ] Compare January's booked days against your capacity. If you're under 60%, add more names from your list and repeat the Week 3 emails.

---

## The daily 20-minute routine

1. Open `outreach-tracker.csv` and sort by `next_step_date`.
2. Send every follow-up that's due today.
3. Send 2-3 new emails from your list.
4. Update `status`, `last_contact` and `next_step_date` for each one.
5. If anything changed, update `q1-booking-calendar.csv`.

## How many emails is enough?

There's no fixed reply rate you can count on; it depends on your field and how warm your list is. Track your own numbers in the tracker. A practical rule: keep sending until your January booked + tentative days reach your capacity, then stop and confirm.

# Worked Example: One Designer's Six Weeks

This is a made-up but realistic example to show how the plan, emails and spreadsheets fit together. The person and clients are fictional, and the results are an illustration, not a prediction of what you'll get.

**Who:** Maya, a freelance graphic designer. Day rate $550. Works 4 billable days a week.
**Starting point (November 14):** One current project ending December 12. Nothing booked for January or February.

---

## Week 1: The list and the calendar

Maya fills in `outreach-tracker.csv`:

| Group | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| current | 4 | The bakery chain (current project), a nonprofit, two agencies that send overflow work |
| past | 13 | Clients from the last two years |
| lead | 7 | People who asked for quotes and went quiet |
| **Total** | **24** | |

She fills in `q1-booking-calendar.csv`: 8 weeks across January and February, 4 days each, minus 1 day for a public holiday and 1 day for her own admin week in February. **Capacity: 30 days.**

She decides to offer a prepaid block: **5 days at a 5% discount, use by March 31.** Normal price $2,750, prepaid price $2,612.50.

## Week 2: Current clients

- **The nonprofit** gets Email 1 (year-end budget) with two suggestions: an annual report cover and a set of donation-page graphics. Reply in two days: yes to the graphics, 2 days of work in December.
- **The bakery chain** gets Email 2 (Q1 planning), suggesting the spring menu boards. They book a 20-minute call.
- **Agency A** replies to Email 2: "Probably need help in late January, will confirm." Marked **tentative**, 4 days.
- **Agency B** doesn't reply.

## Week 3: Past clients and leads

Maya sends Email 3 to all 13 past clients and Email 4 to all 7 leads, a few per day, each with a real first line.

- 6 of 20 reply.
- 2 past clients want small jobs in January (1 day and 2 days). **Booked.**
- 1 lead wants a website refresh "in February, maybe". **Tentative**, 6 days.
- 3 say "not right now". Maya sets a `next_step_date` in April for each.
- Agency B gets Email 6 (gentle follow-up). Still no reply.

The bakery call goes well: spring menu boards, 6 days starting January 12. **Booked.**

## Week 4: Holding dates

- Maya sends Email 7 (hold the dates) to Agency A and the website lead, each with a confirm-by date 8 days away.
- Agency A confirms. **Booked**, 4 days.
- The nonprofit asks about using leftover budget. Maya offers the prepaid block. They buy it: **$2,612.50 invoiced December 8**, to use for their spring campaign.
- Email 5 (holiday hours) goes to everyone with a booked or tentative project.

## Week 5: Last call

- The website lead hasn't confirmed by the deadline. Maya sends Email 8 and releases the hold. Two days later they reply: "Sorry, yes, please book us for February." **Booked**, 6 days.
- Agency B never replies. Marked "no reply", next step January 8.

## Week 6: January

Email 9 goes to all five booked clients with start dates and a list of what she needs.

## The results

| | Days | Value |
|---|---|---|
| December extra work (nonprofit graphics) | 2 | $1,100 |
| January-February booked work | 19 | $10,450 |
| Prepaid block (nonprofit, used in Q1) | 5 | $2,612.50 |
| **Total Q1 days committed** | **24 of 30** | |
| **Total value** | | **$14,162.50** |

How the booked 19 days break down: bakery 6 + Agency A 4 + past client 1 + past client 2 + website lead 6 = 19 days × $550 = $10,450.

Q1 utilization: 24 ÷ 30 = **80%**. That leaves 6 days open, which Maya fills from her Week 6 follow-ups or keeps as a buffer.

## What made the difference

1. **Specific suggestions.** Every reply that turned into work was to an email that named a real project.
2. **Confirm-by dates.** The two tentative projects only became bookings once there was a deadline.
3. **Releasing the hold.** Telling the website lead the dates were released prompted the yes.
4. **Time spent:** about 25 minutes a day for six weeks, roughly 12 hours in total.
